candidates.summary: Anthropic published a Claude Platform guide (Diane Sarkis, Oct 22) recommending that enterprises fold routers, planners and domain subagents into one main agent loop with progressively disclosed skills and tools, plus an Apache-2.0 migration kit. It is resurfacing widely on X today.
facts: Anthropic says that in comparisons across several enterprise deployments, a single agent with skills frequently outperformed both the one-prompt-for-everything design and the subagent design on quality, often at lower cost and latency per task.
One customer that compared its multi-agent harness with a single agent loop saw roughly 2x faster runtime with the single loop.

Anthropic still recommends subagents when a single loop shows measurable degradation from context bloat, when tasks need parallel fresh context windows, or when one agent struggles to select tools or has conflicting instructions.
The guide warns that agent architectures often become a copy of the org chart, with each team shipping its own subagent.
Anthropic released a migration kit at github.com/anthropics/single-agent-loop-kit with a guided workflow and a demo on a mock system.

candidates.summary: Cerebras explained how it serves multi-trillion-parameter models across multiple WSE-3T wafers at 1,000-2,000+ tokens per second, using the open-source ~3T-parameter Kimi K3 as the example. The post reached 303 points on Hacker News.
facts: A single WSE-3T wafer has 44 GB of on-chip memory.
Kimi K3 example: 69 linear-attention layers and 24 dense layers, 4-bit weights, 8-bit KV cache, about 16 GB per layer.
Cerebras places one dense layer per wafer (rest of SRAM for KV cache) and two linear layers per wafer, for 59 wafers total.
Only activations move between wafers, over RDMA over Ethernet at roughly 2 microseconds per hop.
Cerebras cites Kimi K3 at 88.3% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 vs 88.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol.

candidates.summary: An arXiv paper (Clark, Martin, Mahowald) finds AI-generated text uses features linked to human processing difficulty more often than human writing, and hypothesizes that training for math, code and reasoning pushes models toward information density over communication. It reached 231 points on Hacker News.
facts: All nine frontier and near-frontier models studied use more inanimate subjects with animate verbs and more low-frequency n-grams than human writing.
Most also use longer dependencies, more stacked nouns and more reduced object relatives in conversation, with substantial variation across model families.
The authors test their hypothesis with a proof-of-concept fine-tuning experiment.
